title: PostgreSQL: relational & SQL basics
description: Tables, keys, relationships, normalization and the four kinds of SQL commands, the vocabulary every PostgreSQL answer builds on.
source: Study notes: when and how to use PostgreSQL in system design interviews

questions.prompt: What does a foreign key such as REFERENCES users(id) on posts.user_id give you?

options.text: The database rejects a post whose user does not exist.
options.why: Right: referential integrity is enforced by the database.

options.text: A faster full-text search over the contents of every post.
options.why: Foreign keys are about integrity, not search speed.

options.text: Automatic copies of each user row inside every post row.
options.why: It references the user; it does not copy data.

options.text: Permission for any user to edit any other user's posts.
options.why: Access control is a separate concern (GRANT and REVOKE).

questions.explanation: Foreign keys make invalid references impossible, one of the main advantages over schemaless stores.

questions.prompt: Users and the posts they write are an example of which relationship?

options.text: One-to-many: one user can have many posts.
options.why: Right: each post has one author, each user many posts.

options.text: One-to-one: each user has exactly one post.
options.why: That would limit users to a single post.

options.text: Many-to-many: every post belongs to many authors.
options.why: Many-to-many needs a join table and fits likes, not authorship here.

options.text: No relationship, because they live in different tables.
options.why: Separate tables joined by a key are exactly how relationships are modelled.

questions.explanation: Name the cardinality when you draw the schema: one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many.

questions.prompt: Users can like many posts and a post can be liked by many users. How do you model this?

options.text: A likes table with user_id and post_id, keyed on the pair.
options.why: Right: a join table with a composite primary key.

options.text: A comma-separated list of post ids in each user row.
options.why: It breaks integrity, indexing and querying by post.

options.text: A single likes column on the posts table holding one user id.
options.why: That allows only one liker per post.

options.text: One new table per post, each listing the users who liked it.
options.why: Tables per post do not scale and cannot be queried uniformly.

questions.explanation: Many-to-many relationships become a join table. The composite key also stops a user liking the same post twice.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of normalizing data into separate related tables?

options.text: No duplicated data, so an update to one fact happens in one place.
options.why: Right: single source of truth and fewer anomalies.

options.text: Every query becomes faster because there are fewer rows per table.
options.why: Normalization often adds joins; it is not always faster.

options.text: The database no longer needs indexes of any kind.
options.why: Indexes are still required for efficient lookups.

options.text: Transactions are no longer required to keep data consistent.
options.why: Related updates across tables still benefit from transactions.

questions.explanation: Normalize for integrity and flexibility, then denormalize deliberately where reads need it.

questions.prompt: A feed page shows a like count for every post. When is storing like_count on the posts row a sensible denormalization?

options.text: When counting likes per request is too costly and slight staleness is acceptable.
options.why: Right: trade strict consistency for cheaper reads, knowingly.

options.text: Never, because duplicated data is always a design error.
options.why: Deliberate denormalization is a standard performance technique.

options.text: Only when the likes table has been dropped entirely.
options.why: You normally keep the likes table as the source of truth.

options.text: Only when the database runs on a single machine.
options.why: The trade-off exists on any deployment.

questions.explanation: Say the trade-off out loud: the counter can drift, so keep the likes table as truth and update the count transactionally or asynchronously.

questions.prompt: Select all statements that belong to DML (data manipulation) rather than DDL.

options.text: SELECT
options.why: Yes: reading data is DML.

options.text: INSERT
options.why: Yes: adding rows is DML.

options.text: UPDATE
options.why: Yes: changing rows is DML.

options.text: CREATE TABLE
options.why: That is DDL: it defines structure, not row data.

questions.explanation: DDL defines structure (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML works with rows, DCL grants access, TCL controls transactions.

questions.prompt: Which category do BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK belong to?

options.text: TCL, transaction control language.
options.why: Right: they delimit and end transactions.

options.text: DCL, data control language.
options.why: DCL is GRANT and REVOKE for permissions.

options.text: DDL, data definition language.
options.why: DDL changes schema objects, not transaction boundaries.

options.text: DQL, the language that only reads data.
options.why: These statements change the transaction state, not query data.

questions.explanation: DDL defines, DML manipulates, DCL controls access, TCL controls transactions.

questions.prompt: True or false: system design interviews usually test whether you can recall exact SQL syntax rather than choose indexes and access patterns.

options.text: True
options.why: Syntax recall is rarely the point.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: access patterns and indexes matter more than syntax.

questions.explanation: You rarely write SQL; expect questions like which indexes you would create. Junior roles may ask for a basic query.
